packages.hook: I automated a local coffee shop's customer DMs with ChatGPT and a free no-code tool. Not a magic bot — a draft machine. In this video you'll see the exact build, the time it saved, and the three moments it still needed a human.
packages.hook_zh: 我用 ChatGPT 和一个免费无代码工具，把一家本地咖啡店的客户私信自动化了。不是魔法机器人，而是一台『草稿机』。这条视频里你会看到完整搭建、它省下的时间，以及它仍然离不开真人的 3 个瞬间。

hook_options.en: If you run a small business and spend two hours every night answering the same five questions, this is the video. I built one automation that handles the repeat questions and hands you a ready-to-send draft — and I'll show the exact spots where you still have to step in.
hook_options.zh: 如果你开个小生意，每天晚上花两小时回答同一批问题，看这条。我做了一个自动化来处理重复问题，交给你一份可以直接发的草稿——而且我会把你必须亲自出手的那些地方也展示出来。

hook_options.label: 打破『AI 自动化视频都只给你看成片』
hook_options.en: Most 'AI automation' videos lie to you. They show the win and cut the part where the bot sends a wrong price to a real customer. I kept the failure in. Here's an automation that actually runs, plus the three guardrails that stop it from embarrassing you.
hook_options.zh: 大多数『AI 自动化』视频都在骗你。它们只给你看成片，剪掉了机器人把错误价格发给真客户的那段。我把翻车留下了。这是一个真能跑的自动化，外加三道防止它让你社死的护栏。

hook_options.label: 明确交付：提示词+接线+时间账+成本账
hook_options.en: In one afternoon I cut a small shop's inbox time from 90 minutes a day to about 12. You'll get the full ChatGPT prompt, the free automation wiring, a time log, and a cost breakdown you can copy — no agency, no coding degree.
hook_options.zh: 一个下午，我把一家小店收件箱的时间从每天 90 分钟砍到约 12 分钟。你会拿到完整的 ChatGPT 提示词、免费的自动化接线、时间记录，还有一份可以照抄的成本账——没有中介，不需要会写代码。

script.en: Two hours. That's how long a friend who owns a small coffee shop spent every single night answering the same five customer questions. Today I'm using ChatGPT plus one free no-code automation to turn that pile of DMs into ready-to-send drafts. No agency, no coding degree, and I'm keeping the messy failures in the video too.
script.zh: 两小时。这是我一个开咖啡店的朋友，每天晚上回答那五个相同客户问题所花的时间。今天我用 ChatGPT 加一个免费的无代码自动化，把那堆私信变成可以直接发的草稿。没有中介公司，不需要会写代码，而且视频里我会把翻车的部分也留着。
script.viz: 开场亮出两小时夜班痛点
script.img_en: casual creator, early 20s, wearing a grey hoodie and jeans, sitting at a messy desk with a laptop showing a crowded inbox of unread customer messages, warm room light, leaning toward camera with a tired-but-amused expression, smartphone in hand, relatable creator-next-door vibe, candid documentary shot, 35mm lens, shallow depth of field, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 休闲创作者，20 出头，穿灰色连帽卫衣和牛仔裤，坐在乱糟糟的桌前，笔记本上是一堆未读客户消息，暖色房间灯，身体前倾对着镜头，疲惫又带点好笑的表情，手里拿手机，邻家创作者质感，纪实感抓拍，35mm 镜头，浅景深，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Here's the promise. By the end you'll have a repeatable system that reads a new message, drafts a reply in your brand voice, and drops it into a folder for a human to approve. We are not replacing you. We are deleting the boring first pass so you only make the judgment calls. The tool is free up to a generous limit, and each ChatGPT draft costs only a few cents. I tested the whole thing on a real shop's busiest week.
script.zh: 先说承诺。看完你会拿到一套可复用的系统：它读新消息、用你的品牌语气起草回复、再丢进一个文件夹等人确认。我们不是要取代你，而是删掉那个无聊的第一稿，让你只做判断。这个工具在额度内免费，每条 ChatGPT 草稿只要几美分。我是在一家店最忙的一周里实测的。
script.img_en: same casual hoodie creator gesturing at a clean whiteboard that maps three boxes: new message, ChatGPT draft, human approve, with a green checkmark on the human step, bright studio light, confident open-body language, screen recording glow on the laptop behind, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 同一个连帽卫衣创作者，指着一块干净白板，上面画三个框：新消息、ChatGPT 草稿、人工确认，人工那步打了绿勾，明亮棚灯，自信的开放肢体，身后笔记本有录屏微光，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Step one is the trigger. The automation watches a shared inbox label, and anything tagged DM flows in. Step two is the brain. I send the message plus a short brand brief to ChatGPT: who we are, our tone, the five questions we always get, and the real answers. The model returns a draft, never an auto-send. Step three drops that draft into a review queue with the original message attached, so nothing goes out blind. I'll show the exact prompt on screen — and notice it's mostly context, not clever wording.
script.zh: 第一步是触发器。自动化盯着共享收件箱的一个标签，任何标成『私信』的都流进来。第二步是大脑。我把消息加上一段简短的品牌简介发给 ChatGPT：我们是谁、什么语气、那五个总被问到的问题，以及真实答案。模型返回的是草稿，绝不会自动发送。第三步把草稿丢进审核队列，并附上原始消息，所以没有任何东西是盲发的。我会把提示词原样放屏幕上——注意它靠的是上下文，不是华丽的措辞。
script.viz: 搭建第一段：触发器+品牌简介
script.img_en: close-up of the creator's laptop screen showing a no-code automation canvas with three nodes connected by arrows: inbox label trigger, ChatGPT brain node, review queue node, the creator's hand on the trackpad, hoodie sleeve visible, soft desk lamp, crisp UI screenshot style, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 创作者笔记本屏幕特写，无代码自动化画布上三个节点用箭头连接：收件箱标签触发器、ChatGPT 大脑节点、审核队列节点，创作者的手放在触控板上，连帽卫衣袖子可见，柔和台灯，清晰 UI 截图风，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Now wiring it together. The automation takes ChatGPT's draft, files it by question type, and pings one person in Slack with a two-tap approve button. This is the part most videos skip: in my first real run it drafted a reply with last year's price. The guardrail that caught it was a second step that checks the draft against our current price sheet before anything reaches the queue. Automations fail. The question is whether a human sees the mistake before the customer does.
script.zh: 现在把它串起来。自动化把 ChatGPT 的草稿按问题类型归档，并在 Slack 里 ping 一个人，带一个两下点同意的按钮。这正是大多数视频跳过的一段：我第一次真跑的时候，它起草了一条用去年价格的回复。拦住它的是第二步——在任何东西进队列前，先拿草稿和当前价格表比对。自动化会出错。问题是，在客户看到之前，有没有真人看到这个错误。
script.img_en: split screen: left shows a wrong draft with an old price highlighted in red, right shows a guardrail step comparing the draft to a price sheet with a red stop sign, the creator looking concerned shaking head, hoodie, urgent but honest tone, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 分屏：左边一条错误草稿，旧价格被标红；右边一道护栏步骤把草稿和价格表比对，带红色停止标志，创作者皱眉摇头，连帽卫衣，紧迫但诚实的语气，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Let's do the math on the time. Before: ninety minutes a day reading and replying. After: about twelve minutes reviewing drafts and tapping approve. That's roughly eleven hours a week back, almost a full workday. And those twelve minutes aren't grunt work — it's a quick scan while your coffee brews, not the part you dreaded every night. Cost: the automation is free on its tier, ChatGPT runs about two dollars for the whole busy week. So the shop pays two bucks and gets back eleven hours. Even if you value your time at minimum wage, that trade is absurdly one-sided in your favor.
script.zh: 来算时间账。之前：每天 90 分钟阅读加回复。之后：大约 12 分钟审草稿、点同意。一周省回约 11 小时，差不多一个完整工作日。而这 12 分钟不是苦力活——是你咖啡还在煮的那一下快速扫一眼，而不是你每晚都怕的那段。成本：自动化在它的档位里免费，ChatGPT 整个忙周大约 2 美元。所以这家店付 2 美元，换回 11 小时。哪怕你只按最低工资估自己的时间，这笔交换也夸张地偏向你。
script.viz: 数据披露：时间从90分降到12分
script.img_en: creator pointing at a big on-screen bar chart comparing 90 minutes vs 12 minutes per day, with a dollar sign and a clock icon, excited but calm smile, hoodie, calculator app glowing on second monitor, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 创作者指着屏幕上一张大条形图，对比每天 90 分钟 vs 12 分钟，带美元符号和时钟图标，兴奋但平静的微笑，连帽卫衣，副屏上计算器 App 发微光，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: But here are the three places it still needs you. One: any message with a real complaint or a refund needs a human tone, not a template. Two: prices, hours, and menu items change, so the brief has to be updated or the bot drifts. Three: anything legal, like a giveaway rule or a data request, stays with you. The honest pitch isn't 'set it and forget it.' It's 'set it, check it weekly, and you just bought yourself a day.'
script.zh: 但这三个地方它仍然离不开你。一：任何带真实投诉或退款的消息，需要人的语气，不是模板。二：价格、营业时间、菜单会变，所以品牌简介必须更新，否则机器人会跑偏。三：任何法律相关的事，比如抽奖规则或数据请求，都留给你。诚实的说法不是『设好就忘』，而是『设好、每周检查、你就给自己多赚了一天』。
script.img_en: three sticky notes on a laptop lid labeled complaint, price change, legal, each with a small human icon, creator holding up three fingers, hoodie, practical teacher energy, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 笔记本盖上有三张便利贴，分别标着投诉、价格变动、法律，每张带一个小人图标，创作者举起三根手指，连帽卫衣，务实的老师气场，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: What to automate and what not to. Great fit: FAQs, booking confirmations, order-status replies, after-hours first drafts. Bad fit: negotiation, complaints, anything with money moving or a real person's feelings on the line. Start with one inbox label, one question type, and a human in the loop. If it saves you twenty minutes, expand. If it scares you, shrink it. The goal is a smaller to-do list, not a robot you pray works.
script.zh: 该自动化什么、不该自动化什么。适合：常见问题、预约确认、订单状态回复、非工作时间的首稿。不适合：谈判、投诉、任何涉及钱在动或真人情绪的事。从一个收件箱标签、一种问题类型、一个人盯着开始。如果它省了你 20 分钟，就扩；如果它让你害怕，就缩。目标是更短的待办清单，不是一个你祈祷它能工作的机器人。
script.img_en: creator drawing a simple two-column list on a tablet, left column green checkmarks (FAQ, booking, order status), right column red crosses (negotiation, complaints, money), hoodie, focused calm expression, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 创作者在平板上画一个简单的两列清单，左列绿色对勾（常见问题、预约、订单状态），右列红色叉（谈判、投诉、钱），连帽卫衣，专注平静的表情，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: The rule I'd steal: automate the draft, never the send. Let the model write the boring first pass, and keep the human on the last tap. Do that and a two-hour night becomes twelve minutes, every night, forever. If this was useful, smash subscribe and grab the free prompt in the description — I'll keep shipping builds that actually run, failures included. See you in the next one.
script.zh: 我愿意偷走的规则：自动化『草稿』，绝不自动化『发送』。让模型写无聊的第一稿，把最后一下的确认留给真人。做到这点，两小时的夜班就变成 12 分钟，每一晚，一直如此。如果这有用，狠狠点个订阅，去简介拿那个免费提示词——我会继续发那些真能跑、包括翻车在内的搭建。下条见。

packages.hook: Credit card debt in the US just hit about one point three five trillion dollars. But that number means nothing until it's your bill. So I grabbed a real-looking statement — nine thousand four hundred bucks across two cards — and we're going to calculate exactly how much interest you're bleeding, and which payoff order gets you free first.
packages.hook_zh: 美国信用卡债务刚刚到了约 1.35 万亿。但那个数字，只有变成你自己的账单才有意义。所以我拿了一张看起来真实的账单——两张卡共 9400 美元——我们来精确算算你到底在流多少利息，以及哪种还款顺序先让你解脱。

hook_options.label: 戳中『最低还款还了，余额却几乎不动』
hook_options.en: If your statement shows a minimum payment of two hundred bucks but your balance barely moves, you're not bad with money — you're stuck in the minimum-payment trap. In this video I open one real bill and show the exact month your debt actually starts shrinking.
hook_options.zh: 如果你的账单显示最低还款 200 块，但余额几乎不动，你不是不会管钱——你是卡在最低还款陷阱里。这条视频我打开一张真实账单，展示你的债务真正开始缩小的那个月。

hook_options.label: 打破『先还最小那张卡』的直觉
hook_options.en: Everyone says pay off your smallest card first. That feels good but it usually costs you more. I ran the same nine thousand dollars two ways — smallest-first and highest-interest-first — and one of them saved over a thousand dollars and got you free months earlier. The math will annoy you.
hook_options.zh: 大家都说先还最小那张卡。感觉很好，但通常更贵。我把同样的九千美元用两种方式跑了一遍——先小后大、先高利率后低利率——其中一种多省了一千多美元，还让你早几个月解脱。这数学会让你不爽。

hook_options.label: 明确交付：顺序+年限+利息差额
hook_options.en: I'll take a nine-thousand-four-hundred-dollar balance and show you the single change that cuts your payoff time from decades to under two years, and the interest you stop paying. No app to buy, no course — just the order of your payments and one rule about the card.
hook_options.zh: 我拿一个 9400 美元的余额，给你看那一个改动，把还款时间从几十年砍到两年以内，以及你不再付的那笔利息。不用买 App，不用报课——只要改还款顺序，再加一条关于这张卡的规则。

titles: Credit Card Debt Math: One Real Bill, Two Payoff Orders, Which Frees You First
The Minimum Payment Trap — Calculate Exactly When Your Debt Starts Shrinking

script.en: Credit card debt in the US just hit about one point three five trillion dollars. But that giant number means nothing until it's your statement. So I pulled a real-looking bill — nine thousand four hundred dollars across two cards — and we're going to calculate exactly how much interest you're bleeding, and which payoff order gets you free first.
script.zh: 美国信用卡债务刚刚到了约 1.35 万亿。但那个巨大的数字，只有变成你自己的账单才有意义。所以我拿出一张看起来真实的账单——两张卡共 9400 美元——我们来精确算算你到底在流多少利息，以及哪种还款顺序先让你解脱。
script.img_en: calm financial educator in his mid-30s, neat light-blue button-down shirt, seated in a tidy home study with a bookshelf behind, holding a paper credit card statement, soft window light, trustworthy steady expression, a small whiteboard visible, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 沉稳的金融教育者，30 多岁，整洁浅蓝衬衫，坐在整洁书房，背后是书架，手拿一张纸质信用卡账单，柔和窗光，可靠平稳的表情，一块小白板可见，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Meet the example. Take-home pay three thousand two hundred a month. Two cards: a six thousand four hundred balance at twenty-four point nine nine percent, and a three thousand balance at twenty-nine point nine nine. Minimum payments eat about two hundred twenty-five dollars and the balance barely moves. They can throw six hundred a month at the debt. Same numbers, two different orders — and the order changes everything.
script.zh: 认识一下这个例子。到手月收入 3200 美元。两张卡：一张余额 6400、利率 24.99%；一张余额 3000、利率 29.99%。最低还款吃掉约 225 美元，余额几乎不动。他们能每月拿出 600 美元砸向债务。同样的数字，两种不同顺序——而顺序改变一切。
script.img_en: educator at whiteboard writing two card balances and APR percentages with a marker, a simple monthly budget sheet beside, shirt sleeves rolled, clear teacher posture, warm study light, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 教育者在小白板上用马克笔写两张卡余额和利率，旁边一张简单月预算表，衬衫袖子卷起，清晰的老师姿态，暖色书房光，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Two orders. Snowball pays the smallest balance first: minimum on the big card, everything else on the three-thousand one, then roll to the next. Avalanche pays the highest interest first: minimum on the cheaper card, everything on the twenty-nine point nine nine percent one. Snowball feels better because you close a card fast. Avalanche saves more money because interest is a tax you pay every single day you carry a balance. Think of it like this: the snowball is a psychological win, the avalanche is a mathematical win. Most people quit because the math feels slow, so pick the one you'll actually stick with for nineteen months. Same six hundred dollars, opposite logic.
script.zh: 两种顺序。雪球法先还最小余额：大卡还最低，其余全砸那 3000 的，再滚到下一张。雪崩法先还利率最高的：便宜的卡还最低，其余全砸那张 29.99% 的。雪球法感觉更好，因为你很快关掉一张卡。雪崩法省更多钱，因为利息是你每天背着余额就在交的税。这么想：雪球是心理胜利，雪崩是数学胜利。大多数人放弃是因为数学感觉太慢，所以选那个你真的能坚持 19 个月的。同样的 600 美元，相反的逻辑。
script.viz: 雪球 vs 雪崩 解释
script.img_en: whiteboard split into two columns labeled Snowball and Avalanche, each with arrows showing payment flow, educator pointing with a marker, neat shirt, calm explanatory tone, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 小白板分成两列，标着雪球和雪崩，每列有箭头表示还款流向，教育者用马克笔指着，整洁衬衫，平静讲解语气，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Walk the months. Month one, both methods throw six hundred at debt and the balances finally drop instead of creeping. Month three, the avalanche card is visibly smaller because we attacked the twenty-nine percent first. Here's the trap almost everyone hits: they pay extra, feel proud, then swipe the card again for groceries. The payoff plan only works if the card stops being the grocery run. Automate the payment, hide the card, and the math finally gets to breathe. Write the new balance on the fridge every month, so the drop is visible instead of a number buried in an app you never open.
script.zh: 走一遍月份。第一个月，两种方法都砸 600 进去，余额终于下降而不是爬升。第三个月，雪崩那张明显更小，因为我们先打了 29% 的那张。这里是几乎人人会踩的坑：他们还了额外的、觉得骄傲，然后又刷这张卡买菜。还款计划只有在这张卡不再当买菜卡时才有效。把还款设成自动、把卡藏起来，数学才终于能喘气。每月把新余额写在冰箱上，让下降看得见，而不是埋在一个你根本打不开的 App 里。
script.viz: 反转钩子：继续刷卡就白还
script.img_en: educator shaking head at a whiteboard showing a balance that crept back up after a grocery swipe, a red arrow pointing from a shopping cart back to the card, shirt, gentle warning expression, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 教育者在白板前摇头，白板上显示一笔买菜刷卡后余额又爬上去，红色箭头从购物车指回那张卡，衬衫，温和的警告表情，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: The interest math. On this example, paying six hundred a month, the avalanche clears both cards in about nineteen months and costs roughly eleven hundred in interest. Snowball takes about twenty-one months and about thirteen hundred in interest. And if you only ever pay the minimum, the same nine thousand four hundred can linger for thirty years and cost you more in interest than the original balance. The order you pick is worth over a thousand dollars and two months of your life. Run your own numbers with a free calculator — the link is in the description — because your APR and your minimum are almost certainly different from this example.
script.zh: 利息的数学。这个例子里，每月还 600，雪崩法大约 19 个月还清两张卡，利息约 1100。雪球法大约 21 个月、约 1300 利息。而如果你永远只还最低，这同样的 9400 能拖 30 年，利息比本金还多。你选的顺序，值 1000 多美元和两个月的人生。用免费的还款计算器跑你自己的数字——链接在简介里——因为你的利率和最低还款额，几乎肯定和这个例子不一样。
script.viz: 数据披露：19个月 vs 21个月

script.img_zh: 教育者在白板前画时间线：19 个月 vs 21 个月 vs 30 年，加一张利息条形图，平静自信姿势，衬衫，数字被马克笔圈出，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: One tool people reach for: a balance transfer to a zero-percent card. It can cut interest to nothing for twelve to eighteen months — if you actually pay it off in that window and don't treat the old card as free money again. The catch is a transfer fee, usually three to five percent, and the rate snaps back hard if you miss the date. It's a lever, not a cure. Use it only if the math shows you'll be done before the promo ends.
script.zh: 人们常抓的一根稻草：把余额转到 0% 的卡。它能把利息在 12 到 18 个月里降到零——前提是你真的在那个窗口内还清，并且不再把旧卡当免费钱。坑是转账费，通常 3% 到 5%，而且一旦错过日期利率会狠狠弹回。它是个杠杆，不是解药。只有数学显示你能在促销结束前还清时才用。
script.img_en: educator holding a 0 percent offer mailer with a raised eyebrow, a small print box highlighted, shirt, balanced skeptical expression, study bookshelf blurred behind, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 教育者拿着一张 0% 优惠邮件，挑眉，一小块细则被标亮，衬衫，平衡而怀疑的表情，身后书架虚化，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: Quick boundary. This is education, not advice for your exact situation. If the minimum payment is all you can manage, or the balance is growing anyway, talk to a nonprofit credit counselor — in the US, the NFCC can point you to one — before any loan or settlement offer. And never close the card you're paying off just to feel progress; an open, low-balance card helps your score more than an empty closed one.
script.zh: 快速划界。这是教育，不是针对你具体情况的建议。如果最低还款已经是你能做到的全部，或者余额还是在涨，先找一家非营利信用咨询机构——美国的 NFCC 能帮你找到——再考虑任何贷款或和解方案。也永远不要为了『有进展的感觉』去关掉你正在还的卡；一张开着、低余额的卡比一张清空关掉的卡更利于信用分。
script.img_en: educator speaking directly to camera with an open, reassuring hand gesture, a small on-screen line 'Education, not advice', neat shirt, steady trustworthy tone, --ar 16:9 --v 6.0
script.img_zh: 教育者直视镜头，安抚地张开手，屏幕上有一行小字『教育，非建议』，整洁衬衫，平稳可靠的语气，--ar 16:9 --v 6.0

script.en: The one rule: pay the highest interest rate first, automate the payment, and stop using the card while you clear it. Do those three and a balance that felt like a life sentence becomes a line on a spreadsheet you close in under two years. If this helped, subscribe — every week I break one money number down so it finally makes sense. Grab the free payoff calculator link below. See you next time.
script.zh: 唯一规则：先还利率最高的、把还款设成自动、还清前别再用这张卡。做到这三条，一个像无期徒刑一样的余额，就变成一张你在两年内关掉的表格里的一行。如果这有用，订阅——每周我拆一个数字，让它终于讲得通。去下面拿那个免费的还款计算器链接。下条见。

packages.description: US revolving credit hit about $1.35 trillion in mid-2026 — but the only number that matters is your statement. I walk through one example bill: $9,400 across two cards, and calculate exactly how much interest you're bleeding and which payoff order — highest-interest-first vs smallest-first — gets you free sooner. All balances, APRs and payoff times are example calculations using a simple fixed-rate assumption; check your own statement and a calculator before acting. Educational content, not individual financial advice. #creditcarddebt #personalfinance #debtpayoff #financialliteracy
